record.paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
record.original_question: After macroscopic loading and then reverse shear in a soft glassy material, what microscopic or mesoscopic local-yielding asymmetries explain directional memory, also called kinematic hardening or the Bauschinger effect?

evidence.quote: Finally , a key area of focus should be the experimental exploration of the local yielding properties. This entails examining the response at the microscopic or mesoscopic scales, following a loading phase at the macroscopic scale, and during the reverse experiment in which the shear is imposed in the opposite direction. Such investigations can be instrumental in identifying potential asymmetries in the local response, which may elucidate the mechanisms behind directional memory in soft glassy materials.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a soft amorphous (glassy) material — for example a dense emulsion, foam, colloidal glass, or microgel paste — modeled either experimentally or as an assembly of mesoscopic elasto-plastic blocks each carrying a local yield stress and capable of undergoing localized plastic rearrangements ("shear transformations") under an externally imposed simple shear. Subject the material to the following protocol:

1. Apply a macroscopic forward simple shear at fixed strain rate up to (or beyond) the macroscopic yield strain, inducing a population of plastic rearrangements with associated internal stress redistributions.
2. Reverse the direction of the imposed shear and continue deformation in the opposite sense.

It is observed macroscopically that the reverse response is softer than the forward response (kinematic hardening / Bauschinger effect), encoding a directional memory of the prior loading.

Problem: Identify and characterize the microscopic or mesoscopic asymmetries of the local yielding response between the forward and reverse loading phases that are responsible for this directional memory. Concretely:

(a) Define a quantitative measure of local-yielding asymmetry — e.g. the distribution P_+(x) of distances x = (σ_y − σ_loc)/G to the local yield threshold for sites oriented favorably to the forward shear, versus the analogous distribution P_−(x) for sites oriented favorably to the reverse shear — and compute how P_+ and P_− differ after step 1.
(b) Determine how this asymmetry of local thresholds, together with any asymmetry in the residual local stress field and in the rate or spatial organization of plastic rearrangements upon shear reversal, quantitatively reproduces the macroscopic Bauschinger effect.
(c) Specify experimental or numerical observables (at the particle / mesoscopic scale) by which these asymmetries can be measured, and establish the mechanistic relation between the measured local asymmetry and the observed kinematic hardening.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent literature on the Bauschinger effect in amorphous solids (elasto-plastic models, atomistic glass simulations, and colloidal experiments) has identified plausible mechanisms — asymmetric distributions of local yield distances, residual internal-stress fields, and oriented soft spots — but a complete, experimentally validated microscopic explanation of directional memory in soft glassy materials remains an active research question, with no consensus solution.

status_evidence.title: Bauschinger effect in amorphous solids
status_evidence.snippet: Studies elasto-plastic origins of the Bauschinger effect via local yield thresholds and residual stresses in model amorphous solids.
status_evidence.claim: Mechanisms proposed but not fully established.

status_evidence.title: Local yield stress statistics and plasticity in amorphous solids
status_evidence.snippet: Introduces local yield-stress measurements showing directional asymmetries after shear.
status_evidence.claim: Provides tools to measure but not a complete explanation of kinematic hardening in soft glasses.
